A stutter is a disruption in the smooth flow of speech. When someone has a stutter, they cannot speak words out in one clean, continuous stream. Instead, their speech gets interrupted in a specific, involuntary way — they might repeat a sound over and over, get "stuck" on a sound and stretch it out longer than normal, or find themselves completely frozen at a sound with no words coming out at all, even though their mouth is open and they're trying to speak.

The key word here is involuntary. A person with a stutter is not choosing to speak this way. It happens without their control, often despite their best efforts to speak smoothly.

A stutter can show up in three different ways:

1. Repetitions — A sound, syllable, or word gets repeated multiple times before the person can move forward.
Example: "I w-w-w-want some water." (The "w" sound keeps repeating before the word "want" can come out.)

2. Prolongations — A sound gets stretched out unnaturally long.
Example: "Sssssorry I'm late." (The "s" is held for far longer than normal.)

3. Blocks — The person's speech completely freezes. Their mouth may be open, they may be trying, but no sound comes out for a moment before the word finally breaks through.
Example: Imagine someone trying to say "Please" but staying silent with their lips pressed together for two or three seconds before the word comes out.

As a condition (something a person has permanently or over a long period):

  • "He has had a stutter since he was a child."
  • "Her stutter gets worse when she's nervous or excited."
  • "The therapist helped him manage his stutter."

Here, "a stutter" refers to the ongoing speech pattern — a characteristic of how someone speaks.

As a single instance (one specific moment of disrupted speech):

  • "There was a stutter in her voice when she announced the news."
  • "He answered without a single stutter."

Here, "a stutter" refers to one individual interruption or stumble in speech.

The word "stutter" is also used outside of human speech to describe anything that moves or runs in a broken, start-stop, irregular way — just like stuttered speech.

  • "The old engine let out a stutter before finally starting." (The engine coughed and sputtered unevenly.)
  • "There was a stutter in the video — it kept freezing for a split second." (The video playback was interrupted repeatedly.)
  • "The machine moved forward in a stutter." (It moved in short, jerky bursts instead of smoothly.)

The logic is simple: just as a stutter in speech breaks up the smooth flow of words, a stutter in anything else breaks up its smooth, continuous operation.

You will often come across another word — stammer — which describes virtually the same thing. The two words are used interchangeably by most people. The only practical difference is regional: "stutter" is the more common term in American English, while "stammer" is more commonly used in British English. If you encounter both, know that they refer to the same condition.
Important things to understand about a stutter

• A stutter is not caused by low intelligence, shyness, or a lack of confidence. Many highly intelligent and confident people stutter.
  • Stuttering often worsens under pressure — when someone is anxious, excited, tired, or put on the spot, their stutter may become more pronounced. In relaxed situations, the same person might speak almost completely fluently.
  • Many people who stutter speak entirely normally when singing, whispering, or talking to themselves — which shows how the condition is specifically tied to the act of regular, monitored speech.
  • Stuttering can be improved with speech therapy, practice, and certain techniques, though for many people it remains a lifelong characteristic.
  • Having a stutter does not mean a person struggles to think of what to say — they know exactly what they want to say. The difficulty is purely in the physical act of producing the sounds.

A stutter (noun) is either: (1) a speech condition in which a person involuntarily repeats sounds, stretches them out, or freezes on them, disrupting the natural flow of speech; or (2) a single such disruption in speech or in any other process that is meant to run smoothly. It is always unintended and beyond the person's immediate control.
